drills.q: RED or USE: which applies to a connection pool, and which applies to an HTTP endpoint?
drills.a: USE applies to the connection pool (a finite resource). RED applies to the HTTP endpoint (serves discrete requests).

drills.q: How many minutes of downtime per month does a 99.95% SLO allow?
drills.a: 21.6 minutes (0.05% of 43,200 minutes in a 30-day month).

drills.q: A histogram with 10 buckets is tracked across 50 services with no other labels. How many time series does this create in classic (non-native) Prometheus histograms?
drills.a: 500 time series, before adding any further label like region or version.

drills.q: A GPU-serving inference endpoint's request latency has doubled, but GPU utilization metrics look completely normal. What does RED/USE tell you to check next, and why?
drills.a: The disagreement between RED (endpoint latency up) and USE (GPU utilization normal) rules out the GPU itself as the bottleneck and points upstream -- check request queueing before the GPU, batching/scheduling changes, or a different saturated resource in the path (network, preprocessing) that isn't being measured. Instrument the queue itself as its own USE resource.

drills.q: Design a burn-rate alert that pages when a service is on track to exhaust 2% of its 30-day error budget in 1 hour. What burn rate and windows does this correspond to, per the Google SRE Workbook?
drills.a: 14.4x burn rate on a 5-minute short window and a 1-hour long window, both must breach simultaneously (multi-window multi-burn-rate) before paging.

drills.q: An alert fires constantly with no real incident behind it and gets muted by the team within weeks. Diagnose the likely cause and the fix.
drills.a: Likely a single-window threshold alert too sensitive to short blips, or a cause-based (CPU/memory) alert with no real correlation to user impact. Fix: replace with a symptom-based burn-rate alert using multi-window multi-burn-rate to require both current and sustained confirmation.

drills.q: A Grafana dashboard panel takes 20-30 seconds to load. What's the likely cause and the fix?
drills.a: An expensive PromQL aggregation is being computed live on every page load with no recording rule backing it. Fix: add a recording rule that precomputes the aggregation on ingest, and point the panel at the precomputed series.

drills.q: Your team's release velocity has ground to a halt because the error budget is exhausted almost every month within the first week. What's actually wrong, and what are the two possible fixes?
drills.a: Either the SLO target is set stricter than the system's actual reliability supports, or there's a recurring root cause never fixed between windows. Fixes: revisit whether the SLO matches real business criticality, and/or ensure the budget recovers on a rolling window rather than a punitive hard calendar reset -- and separately, root-cause and fix whatever's chronically consuming budget.

drills.q: A team 'fixes' alert fatigue by raising every alert threshold by 20% across the board. Why is this the wrong fix, even though it will reduce page volume?
drills.a: It's tuning, not fixing -- it doesn't address whether each remaining alert is actually actionable or correlated with real user impact, and it risks quietly increasing false negatives (missing real incidents) as a side effect of chasing a lower page count. The real fix is symptom-based burn-rate alerting plus deleting non-actionable alerts.

drills.q: Two teams' dashboards disagree about whether an incident happened last Tuesday. What's the likely root cause, and how does Grafana 13's dashboards-as-code help prevent this?
drills.a: Each team's dashboard likely defines 'success' for the same underlying SLI slightly differently (different latency threshold, different error-code inclusion) with no central source of truth. Git-backed, PR-reviewed dashboards make SLI/SLO definitions explicit, version-controlled, reviewable artifacts instead of tribal knowledge embedded separately in each team's panel config.

drills.q: Should a low-stakes internal admin tool used by 3 employees have a formal SLO/error-budget process with on-call paging? Justify the answer and name the trigger that would change it.
drills.a: No -- the operational cost (on-call burden, engineering time chasing a tight budget) exceeds the actual business impact of occasional downtime for a genuinely low-stakes tool. The trigger to revisit: the moment that tool's blast radius changes, e.g. it gets embedded in a customer-facing workflow -- re-evaluate then, not on a fixed schedule.
